# Hypothesis testing {.hero #s06-testing}

::: {.sem-mark data-sem="6"}
Seminar 6 · p-values and error rates
:::

A p-value answers one question, and it is not the one you want.

::: {.lede}
It does not tell you the probability that $H_0$ is true. It tells you how ordinary your sample would look in a world where $H_0$ *is* true — which is a question about the world, not about your hypothesis.
:::

Nothing here required a table. The p-value is a counting exercise: of all the samples $H_0$ would produce, what share are at least as extreme as ours?

## What $\alpha$ actually buys {.sim-slide #alpha-sim}

::: {.slide-kicker}
Seminar 6 · Type I error
:::

::: {.lede-min}
Below, $H_0$ is **true** in every single one of the 5,000 worlds. Every rejection is therefore a false alarm — so the rejection rate should come out at $\alpha$.
:::

::: {.sim-card .sim-text}
```{webr-r}
alpha <- 0.05   # <-- your significance level
reps  <- 5000
n     <- 30

reject <- replicate(reps, {
  x <- rnorm(n, mean = 100, sd = 15)  # H0 is TRUE
  t <- (mean(x) - 100) / (sd(x)/sqrt(n))
  abs(t) > qt(1 - alpha/2, n - 1)
})
mean(reject)   # how often we cried wolf
```
:::

::: {.try-this}
You get back roughly `alpha`. Set it to `0.01` and the false-alarm rate follows. **$\alpha$ is not a truth threshold — it is the false-alarm rate you have agreed to live with.**
:::

## "Fail to reject" is not "accept" {.sim-slide #power-sim}

::: {.slide-kicker}
Seminar 6 · the other error
:::

:::: {.claim-pair}

::: {.claim-cell .claim-wrong}
[Wrong]{.claim-tag}

"We failed to reject, so the means are equal."

Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence — a small sample fails to reject almost everything.
:::

::: {.claim-cell .claim-right}
[Right]{.claim-tag}

"We had too little evidence to rule equality out."

Whether that is reassuring depends entirely on how much power you had.
:::

::::

::: {.sim-card .sim-text}
```{webr-r}
n <- 10   # <-- try 10, then 50, then 200

# H0 is FALSE here: the true mean is 105, not 100
mean(replicate(4000, {
  x <- rnorm(n, mean = 105, sd = 15)
  t <- (mean(x) - 100) / (sd(x)/sqrt(n))
  abs(t) > qt(0.975, n - 1)
}))
```
:::

::: {.try-this}
At `n <- 10` you detect a real effect about **16%** of the time. Failing to reject told you nothing — the test could barely see. At `n <- 200` it is near certain. **"No significant difference" is only informative once you know the power.**
:::
